review.headline: A solid opening unraveled by a miscalculated tactical sequence

sections.text: You stepped into a Bishop's Opening and defended sensibly with 2...Nf6 and 3...d6. White opted to trade on e6 with 5.Bxe6, and after 5...fxe6, your doubled e-pawns gave you a solid grip on the center and opened the f-file for your rook. Both sides developed smoothly, and by the time you castled with 7...O-O, your position was completely sound.

White decided to challenge the center with 8.d4, and you correctly liquidated with 8...exd4 9.Nxd4. At this moment, your e6-pawn was under pressure from White's knight. A calm developing move like 9...Qd7 would have protected the weakness and kept the game balanced at +0.1.

Instead, you went for 9...Nxe4, which unleashed a discovered attack from your bishop on e7 against White's bishop on g5. The idea to win a pawn and trade pieces was ambitious, but it overlooked White's counter-threat: 10.Nxe6 attacked your queen and rook simultaneously. After 10...Bxg5 11.Nxd8, your queen was lost, and 12.Qd5+ left no hope of recovery.

review.turning_point: The game was decided by 9...Nxe4, which allowed 10.Nxe6 to win your queen rather than just swapping off minor pieces.
review.focus: Before playing an active tactical reply like 9...Nxe4, make sure you address direct attacks against your own tender points, such as the e6-pawn.

review.headline: A messy Philidor defense cut short on the clock

sections.text: You went with the Philidor Defense, but the opening got uncomfortable quickly. After 5.exd6, taking back with 5...cxd6?! left your pawn structure split and your central control loose. White traded on e6 with 7.Bxe6 fxe6, saddling you with doubled e-pawns and giving White an easy runway to target your weaknesses.

White hopped inward with 9.Nd4 and 10.Ne6, eventually grabbing a pawn on g7 with 11.Nxg7+. You had to move your king with 11...Kd8, but you tried to generate counterplay by activating your rook with 12...Rg8 and jumping into the attack with 13...Qh3?!, creating a pin against the g2-pawn with the rook on g8 and queen on h3.

White gave you a golden chance with 14.Qf3?, creating a fork against your queen on h3 and knight on e4. Instead of trading queens with 14...Qxf3, you played 14...Qf5?, which set up a pin on the f4-pawn along the f-file but let White stay in control after 15.fxe5. You continued active defense with 18...Qc5+, but time ran out on move 19.

review.turning_point: The critical moment arrived when White slipped with 14.Qf3?, offering queen trades; missing 14...Qxf3 allowed White to keep the advantage after 15.fxe5.
review.focus: Look for simplifying queen trades when your pieces are under coordinated pressure, rather than retreating with moves like 14...Qf5?.
